lines.text: Toys R Us didn't lose to Amazon. It lost to a loan, one that cost about $400M a year in interest before it sold a single toy.
For decades, it was where American children went to pick their birthday and Christmas presents. Then, in 2018, it began closing every one of its 735 American stores.
As many as 33,000 jobs were at stake. Even Geoffrey, the giraffe on every sign, was out of work.
Most people blame the internet, and Amazon. It's a neat story. But the company's own annual reports tell a different one, and it is written in black and white.
In 2005, three buyers took Toys R Us over for $6.6B. Much of that money was borrowed, and the debt landed on the toy store itself.
Years later, in its last full year, the stores earned $460M. The interest bill came to $457M.
That left $5M before tax, out of $11.54B in sales. Amazon was the weather. The loan was the leak.
Here is how America's toy store lost to its own loan, told from its own filings: the shop, the deal, the buyout, the bill, and the bankruptcy.
Chapter one. How a furniture shop became a toy supermarket.
Where did it start? It began in 1948, in Washington, D.C., when a young man named Charles Lazarus opened a baby furniture store. He called it Children's Bargain Town.
The timing was perfect. After the war, America was having babies at a record pace, and every new family needed a crib, a pram and, a little later, toys.
So why toys? Parents bought a crib once. But as Lazarus later told it, they came back for toys again and again, as their children grew. So he sold more toys, and less furniture.
By 1957, the store had a new name, written with a backwards R, as if a child had spelled it: Toys R Us.
What made it different? The idea was simple. One huge store, stacked to the ceiling with every kind of toy, at discount prices, open all year, not just at Christmas.
In 1978, Toys R Us sold its shares to the public, and used the money to keep opening big stores, in town after town.
When Lazarus retired as chief executive in 1994, the company ran or licensed over 1,000 stores, in 17 countries.
How far did it reach? From its head office in New Jersey to Britain, Germany and Japan, the giraffe was going global.
British shoppers saw the backwards R on retail parks, like this one in Swindon. In Japan, families queued outside for grand openings.
Its mascot was Geoffrey the Giraffe, who turned up at openings and parades. And its jingle told a whole generation of kids they never had to grow up.
Every December, the car parks filled up. Parents brought shopping lists, kids brought wish lists, and the giraffe smiled down from the sign over the door.
What came next? In 1996, it launched Babies R Us, for new parents. Expecting mothers even got their own parking spaces, right by the door.
In New York, its flagship store on Times Square had a full-size Ferris wheel inside it. Tourists queued just to ride it.
It sold the toys a generation grew up with: the Nintendo, the Game Boy, the Lego, the Barbie.
Not every idea worked. It had also opened Kids R Us, a chain of children's clothing stores. In a later annual report, it explained why it had decided to close all 146 that were left.
So how big was it? The main business was huge. In its last full year as a public company, Toys R Us had $11.1B in sales, and it was still one of America's best-known shops.
It owned the toy aisle. But a new kind of store was opening, one with no aisles at all, and no car park. Could the toy supermarket learn to sell online?
Chapter two: a deal with Amazon.
Its annual reports named the rivals it worried about: Walmart, Target, and Amazon.
In the late nineties, the dot-com boom was on. Every big shop wanted a website, and nobody yet knew how to make money from one.
Toys R Us launched its own website in 1998. Selling toys online sounds easy, but every order has to be picked, packed and posted, and in December there are millions of them.
So in 2000, it signed a deal with Amazon to run its online toy store. The annual report called it a strategic alliance.
Amazon built the site, packed the orders and stored the toys in its own warehouses. Toys R Us picked and bought the toys.
The deal was set to run until 2010. On paper, it was the toy store's fast way online, without building a single warehouse. So what could go wrong?
It didn't last. In 2004, Toys R Us sued Amazon, to enforce what it called its exclusive rights under the agreement. Other sellers were offering toys on the same site.
What was the fight about? Toys R Us said the deal was meant to make it the main toy seller on Amazon's site. Then it found other sellers offering toys there too.
Amazon sued back, saying the toy store had not kept enough toys in stock. In 2006, a New Jersey court let Toys R Us end the deal.
For years, people who typed in the toy store's web address had really been shopping on Amazon's site, with Amazon handling their orders.
People were already shopping there online. The company counted more than 120M visits to its websites in a single year.
Now Toys R Us had to run that online store on its own, while Amazon, which had learned the toy business from the inside, kept selling toys.
But by then, a bigger change had already begun, and it had nothing to do with the internet. It was about who owned the company, and how they paid for it.
Chapter three, and the turning point: the buyout.
In July 2005, three owners took Toys R Us private: the investment firms KKR and Bain Capital, and the property company Vornado.
What does going private mean? It meant its shares came off the stock market. From now on, a small group of owners would make the big decisions, away from the public.
How much did they pay? The price was $6.6B. The company's annual report still records the deal, years later.
It was what's called a leveraged buyout. The buyers put in some money of their own, and borrowed much of the rest.

On paper the plan is simple. Buy a company mostly with borrowed money, let its profits pay the interest, improve it, then sell it for more. When it works, the owners make a fortune on a small stake. When it doesn't, the company is left holding the debt.
Sounds abstract? Think of buying a house with a big mortgage. Except here, the mortgage isn't yours. It belongs to the house, and the house has to pay it.

That was the catch. The debt was not the buyers' to repay. It sat on the books of Toys R Us, and the stores had to earn the money to pay it. That is how a leveraged buyout works, and why the store itself carries the risk.
And who pays when it goes wrong? Not only the lenders, and not only the owners. The workers, the suppliers and the shoppers feel it too.
The next annual report said it plainly. Because of the borrowing, interest costs would remain high for the foreseeable future.
Was that all? No. The owners also charged the company an advisory fee: $17M a year, later cut to $6M. The fee shrank. The interest bill did not.
By its last annual report, the owners' funds held 98% of the voting shares. They controlled the company, and the filing warned their interests might not match its own.
The same filing listed that as a risk. The owners might chase deals that helped their own investments, even if those deals carried risks for the company.
The usual plan in a buyout is to fix the company and sell it on. In 2010, Toys R Us filed papers to sell its shares to the public again.
The sale never happened. Toys R Us stayed private, and the debt stayed on its books, year after year.
New owners, a big debt, and toy shoppers starting to buy online. So what did that debt actually cost, every single year?
A quick recap. A toy empire built over decades, an online deal that ended in court, and a buyout paid for with borrowed money. Now comes the bill.
Chapter four. Every year, a bill.
Before the buyout, in its last full year as a public company, Toys R Us paid $130M in interest.
The year of the buyout, that bill jumped to $394M. The year after, it reached $537M.
And it never came back down. Every year after that, the interest stayed between $419M at its lowest, and $524M at its highest.
How big is that, really? Spread across every store it ran, each one had to send hundreds of thousands of dollars a year to the lenders, before paying a single worker or fixing a single light.
Measured against sales, the change looks small: interest went from 1.2% of sales to 3.5%. But in retail, where profits are thin, that difference is enormous.
That's a bill that arrives whether the shop has a good Christmas or a bad one, whether the toys sell or sit on the shelf.
Add those years up, and the interest alone came to billions of dollars. Money that went to lenders, not to the stores.
And the stores kept selling. In its last full year, Toys R Us still sold $11.54B worth of toys and baby products, across 1,691 stores it ran itself.
So were the stores the problem? Those stores earned $460M, before any interest was paid. A healthy shop, on the face of it.
And then the interest took $457M. That's 99% of everything the stores earned, gone to the lenders.
Think of it this way. For almost every dollar the stores earned, a dollar went straight back out of the door, to pay interest on the loan.
What was left before tax: $5M. On $11.54B of sales. Almost nothing.
Before the buyout, interest took 43% of what the stores earned. In the last full year, it took nearly all of it.
That was the leak. In most years the stores made money. The loan took most of it, and in some years more than all of it, before anything could be spent on making the stores better.
The company's own filing warned what the debt meant: less cash left to run its stores and grow the business.
Shoppers could see it in the aisles. And as more of them bought online, the gap between the toy store and its rivals kept growing.

Again and again, the company borrowed new money to pay off old loans as they came due. Each new loan came with its own interest, and lending to a company already deep in debt is rarely cheap. It bought time. It never made the debt go away.
In its last years, a new chief executive, David Brandon, came in to fix things. The annual report listed his plans: better service in the stores, and a stronger financial foundation.
For years, it was just enough to keep going. Then, in 2017, the cash ran short, right before Christmas.
Chapter five. Bankruptcy, before Christmas.
Why then? It needed money to stock its shelves for the holidays. Its advisers tried to raise at least $200M, just to make it to January.
It talked with lenders holding part of a $1B loan about a deal to raise cash. They ran out of time.
According to the court filings, it had spent months looking for a way out from under its debt. None of the deals came together.
Then, in early September, news reports said it might go bankrupt.
Why does a rumour matter so much? Because a toy store does a huge part of its business in a few weeks at the end of the year, and it has to buy those toys months before, on credit from its suppliers.
Suppliers got nervous. Afraid they wouldn't be paid, some held back their shipments. And a toy store without new toys before Christmas is in real trouble.
On a Monday in September 2017, Toys R Us filed for Chapter Eleven bankruptcy protection, in Richmond, Virginia.
It owed $5.2B, and ran about 1,600 stores around the world.
How big was it? Reuters called it the biggest bankruptcy of an American retailer since Kmart's, more than a decade earlier.
And it took investors by surprise. No big debt payment was due right away. The company simply couldn't get the cash in time for Christmas.
Could it still be saved? The court let it borrow more than $2B to pay suppliers, so it could stock up on toys like Lego and Barbie for Christmas.
For a few weeks, it looked like it might work. The shelves were stocked, the stores were open, and the company was still selling toys to families doing their holiday shopping.
It said it would keep its stores open while it fixed its debt. The doors stayed open, and the giraffe stayed on the signs.
Here's where we are: a loan that took nearly everything the stores earned, and a bankruptcy filed just before Christmas. Next came the holiday season that was supposed to save it.
Chapter six. Closing time.
After the holidays, no rescue came. In March 2018, Toys R Us asked the court to let it sell off everything, in all 735 of its American stores.
Chapter Eleven is meant to let a company keep trading while it cuts its debt. Toys R Us couldn't make that work. So it moved to liquidation: sell the stock, close the stores, pay back what it could.
Who paid the price? As many as 33,000 jobs were at stake, in stores across the country. Cashiers, stock workers, managers.
In its statement, the company called it a profoundly sad day, for itself and for the families it had served for 70 years.
Shelves emptied. Signs went up. Everything must go. Shoppers came for the bargains, and some came just to say goodbye.
By that summer, the last American stores had closed their doors. The toy supermarket was gone from the country that invented it.
Geoffrey came down from the signs. For a lot of grown-ups who had walked those aisles as children, it felt like a piece of their childhood had closed too.

Many of the buildings still stand. Some were taken over by other shops. Others are still empty years later. If you grew up near one, there is a good chance the building is still there, wearing another company's sign.
On some walls, you can still see the outline of the old sign, where the letters used to hang.
That was the end in America. But outside the United States, the story didn't end the same way everywhere.
Chapter seven. Outside America.
Did the rest of the world go down too? Not all of it. In Britain, Toys R Us went into administration just weeks before the American closures, with 105 stores and more than 3,000 jobs.
No buyer came. Every British store closed that spring, and the big sheds on the retail parks were left for other shops.
In Canada, it went differently. Its 82 Canadian stores drew a bidder and kept trading for years, until the Canadian chain ran into debt trouble of its own.
Shoppers in Quebec, like these in Montreal, could still walk into a Toys R Us, years after the American stores had gone.
In Asia, the stores kept trading too, in places like Japan and Hong Kong, run by a separate company.
So in parts of the world, the giraffe lasted. The ending in America was not the only ending.
Even in America, the name came back. New owners licensed it, and opened Toys R Us shops inside Macy's department stores, and at airports.
But they were small shops inside other stores, not the toy supermarkets of the past.
What really brought down Toys R Us in America? And what does it teach anyone who runs, or buys, a business?
Chapter eight. Looking back at what really happened, and what it means.
So was it the online giant after all? The competition was real. Walmart, Target and Amazon all sold the same toys, often cheaper, and more shoppers bought them online every year.
But every toy seller faced that weather. Toys R Us faced it while its interest bill took 99% of what its stores earned.
That is the whole story in one line. A loan can't be outsold. The stores sold $11.54B of toys in a year, and still couldn't get ahead of the interest.
Would it have lasted without the loan? Nobody can say for sure. But in its last full year, its stores earned $460M. Before the buyout, its whole interest bill was $130M.
Three lessons. First: a business can be busy and still go broke, if the debt takes the profit.
Second: who owns a company, and how they paid for it, can matter more than what it sells. The same stores, with a lighter loan, might have had a very different ending.
Third: when money runs short, suppliers notice first. They see the late payments before the public sees anything. Once they hold back shipments, the end can come very fast.

Here it is, start to finish. A furniture shop became a toy giant. The internet arrived, and an online deal ended in court. Then a buyout loaded the company with debt, the interest ate the profits year after year, and one Christmas the cash ran out.
Over to you. Did you have a favourite Toys R Us aisle, or a toy you still remember buying there? Tell us which one in the comments, and what you bought there.
That was the story of Toys R Us, told from the public record.
